title: The Cutileiro Plan and the Lisbon Agreement
sources: Burg & Shoup, The War in Bosnia-Herzegovina (1999), Chapter 3 on the European Community mediation
ICTY Karadzic Trial Judgment (IT-95-5/18-T), context on pre-war negotiations
European Community Conference on Yugoslavia, statements of principles February-March 1992
Balkan Battlegrounds Vol. I, pre-war diplomatic context
content:
By the end of 1991, the European Community had taken on the principal mediating role in the unfolding Yugoslav crisis. The Hague Conference on Yugoslavia, established in September of that year under the chairmanship of Lord Carrington, had begun to address the configuration of relations among the federation's constituent republics. The Bosnian dimension of that work was delegated to a Portuguese diplomat, José Cutileiro, then the Portuguese Ambassador in London, whose government held the rotating EC presidency. Cutileiro's mandate was to facilitate negotiations among the three principal Bosnian political parties — the Party of Democratic Action (SDA) led by Alija Izetbegović, the Serbian Democratic Party (SDS) led by Radovan Karadžić, and the Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ) of Bosnia and Herzegovina led by Mate Boban — on a constitutional arrangement that might preserve Bosnia and Herzegovina as a single political unit.

Cutileiro's approach centred on a proposed framework that came to be known as the Statement of Principles for New Constitutional Arrangements for Bosnia and Herzegovina, agreed in Lisbon on 23 February 1992. The framework envisaged Bosnia as a state composed of three constituent units defined by ethnic majorities, with significant powers devolved to those units and a central government with limited but real authority. Maps proposed under the framework would have allocated municipalities to one or another of the constituent units according to the ethnic majority of their pre-war population, with provisions for shared sovereignty in mixed areas and arrangements for protection of minorities within each unit.

The framework was, in the immediate aftermath of the Lisbon meeting, accepted in principle by representatives of all three parties — including Izetbegović, who initialled the agreement. Within ten days, however, Izetbegović had publicly withdrawn his support, citing concerns that the proposed cantonal arrangement would produce de facto partition of the republic and that the principle of ethnic constitution would entrench the categories that had become the organising principle of the unfolding crisis. The withdrawal was not a unilateral or ill-considered act; it followed consultations within the SDA leadership and was reportedly informed by signals received from the United States Ambassador to Yugoslavia, Warren Zimmermann, who indicated that Washington's preference was for an internationally recognised Bosnia within its existing borders rather than a partitioned settlement.

The withdrawal produced an extended period of subsequent negotiations through March and into early April. Cutileiro continued to mediate, producing successive iterations of the framework with adjustments to the maps and to the powers allocated to the central government. None of the iterations succeeded in restoring Izetbegović's support. The European Community recognised Bosnia and Herzegovina's independence on 6 April 1992; the United States followed the next day. By that point, the Cutileiro framework had effectively been overtaken by events.

The historical assessment of the Cutileiro framework has been one of the war's recurring counterfactual debates. Some accounts — Burg and Shoup among them — treat the framework as a serious diplomatic effort whose rejection contributed to the war that followed and whose substance, in retrospect, anticipated arrangements that the Dayton settlement would later codify. Other accounts emphasise the asymmetries embedded in the framework: that it accepted the principle of ethnic constituency on terms that the Bosnian Serb leadership had been advocating; that the maps it proposed were drawn on the assumption that local ethnic majorities should determine sovereign authority, an assumption that the war's subsequent campaign of expulsions would render untenable as a basis for legitimacy.

The Karadžić Trial Judgment treated the Cutileiro period in the context of pre-war preparations by the Bosnian Serb leadership for the establishment of the Republika Srpska. The chamber's findings on the Strategic Objectives and on the formation of the SDS Crisis Staffs and the Republika Srpska military and political structures pre-dated the Cutileiro framework's collapse. Whatever the framework's diplomatic merits, the chamber found, the Bosnian Serb leadership had been pursuing a parallel track of preparations for the territorial separation of Serb-claimed regions of Bosnia that the negotiations had not arrested and that the framework's cantonal logic had not, in operational terms, dissuaded.

The Lisbon agreement and its collapse remain among the most discussed episodes of the war's diplomatic prologue, a case in which the documentary record is clear, the chronology is established, and the interpretation of cause and consequence remains contested.
